title: Anamnesis project tracker
about: A public project tracker for the Anamnesis successor design: what it is for, how it is built and with what, then every decision, option, test and task, with its status and evidence. It leaves out the corpus, secrets, deployment-specific material and the owner's own words.

goal.lede: Anamnesis is the machinery an AI persona, Nyx, uses to remember and to have continuity. She works across hundreds of sessions, runs sub-agents, talks mostly with one human now and with many interlocutors later, and will carry herself from a workstation to other mediums. Her memory has to outlive the session, the model, the machine and the medium, and be one she can trust. Identity is a sibling project, Daimon; this one is the memory. It is built for her, and the machinery is for anyone who wants it. The current engine works, but it is built the wrong way round. It treats distilled facts as beliefs, so every fact must be right and every stale one must be found and hidden, and most of its machinery exists to do that. The successor is a redesign around what the cited evidence and the measurements here point to: episodes are the answer, facts only help find them, and currency is shown to the reader instead of being settled by hiding things.
goal.problems_head: What is wrong today, as measured

problems.text: Ranking carries no currency signal. When both versions of a changed fact were retrieved, the older one ranked first in 22 of 27. The questions were phrased from the old fact, so ranking follows the question's wording, and similarity expansion does not fix it.
Identity is a file position. With the current parsers, adding an id anywhere in the journal re-hashes 779 or 780 of its 780 entries.
Five stores and a separate hash chain share no write lock outside the nightly run (from an audit, not reproduced), and 118 of 280 entry headers named a time ahead of the clock.
Memory rarely reaches a session through recall. Over 30 days, 36% of sessions grepped the raw journal and 7% called recall, while roughly 260 KB loads into every session.
What gets written is not checked enough. A review found 10 of 74 auto-authored entries with an unsupported claim, and 1 of 20 after the fix.
It is coupled to specific models. Thresholds fitted to specific quantised models break silently on a swap, and every writing stage hangs on one login.
The agent now reads an untrusted social network, so what it writes into memory can be poisoned. On the survey's reading, the only defence with evidence is provenance assigned by code at write time.

aims.text: Answer with evidence. Every recalled memory comes back as a dated episode with its evidence and a rope to its transcript.
Show currency and hide nothing. A reader sees the timeline newest first, and an outdated fact is marked, not removed.
Lose nothing. The transcript stays the ground truth, every derived store rebuilds from it, and only three logged doors remove anything.
Survive a change of model, vendor or machine. A swap is a re-test against a gate, not a rewrite.
Usable by anyone. The core names roles and never a persona; whatever is particular to one persona lives in its deployment profile.
Go where she goes. Any number of machines and mediums, from workstation to laptop to phone and beyond, each writing its own segment, merging as a union.
Know who said it. Every episode says who each interlocutor was, and what one interlocutor may be shown of what another said is decided, not left to chance.
Resist poisoning. Origin is assigned by code at write time, never by a model.
Be smaller. The design counts 40 mechanisms against today's 50.
Beat the current engine on a private gold set, against bars written before anything is built.

non_goals.text: Not a product or a benchmark entry. Public benchmarks run, if at all, only as sanity checks.
Not forgetting. Nothing is dropped by decay or to save space.
Not shared ownership. It is one persona's memory; the people, agents and personas she talks with appear in it as interlocutors, never as its owners.
Not the identity. How the persona is defined, carried, protected and re-aligned is the sibling project, Daimon; this one is the memory.
Not tied to one model, vendor or machine.
Not closed. Everything but the corpus and secrets is public, external research is credited, and the project's own research is free to all.

architecture.lede: What is being built: a memory engine in which the transcript is the only ground truth and everything above it is derived and can be rebuilt from it. A memory is made once, through one writer, and each item in its Record is checked against its transcript, where one exists, before the file is created. It is kept as an immutable episode file. Facts are keys that find episodes, a ledger records every derived decision, and a disposable projection serves recall. Labels decide where content may flow, never whether it is kept, and only three logged doors ever remove anything.
architecture.layers_head: Six layers, and what lives in git
architecture.map_note: Each box links to the item that decides it and takes that item's status, so the map changes when a decision does. Read the lanes in order: sources, making, keeping, serving.

rules.text: Transcripts are the only ground truth. Everything above them is derived and can be rebuilt.
One writer. Every episode is born through the same append, created atomically and never rewritten by a machine.
Record items are checked against the transcript before the file exists, and a fact the memory relies on must be in the Record, not only in the prose.
Facts are keys into episodes, never beliefs. Recall answers with the episode and its evidence.
Roles, not models. A filler that passes the gate fills the role, and a replacement passes it again.
Profiles, not personas. The core names roles and never a persona; whatever is particular to one lives in its deployment profile.
Labels route, never filter. They decide where content may flow, never whether it is kept.
Nothing in the cache is the only copy of anything, and recall writes nothing outside it.
Nothing is deleted silently. Only three logged doors remove anything.

flow.text: A session runs, and the harness writes its transcript (L0).
A producer reads the screened transcript and drafts typed items. In session, the author drafts and code pre-fills what code can know.
The credential screen redacts live credentials, the label classifier adds labels, and the verifier checks every quote and anchor against the transcript.
The writer creates the episode file atomically. A failing item is withheld on its own.
The ledger records what was derived, facts are extracted as keys, and the projection is rebuilt from the episodes and the ledger.

A session receives memory through the start pack, recall or the raw files. Recall shows each hit with its evidence, date and age; a grep of the raw files shows none of that, which is what D3 is about.
P3 promotes what passes its gates into canon, and the signer signs the daily root.
Anything wrong leaves only through invalidate, redact or purge, and each door is logged.

technology.lede: Most choices are deliberately plain: the current engine's measured core, kept until a local challenger beats it on the gold set, and SQLite with plain files, which the survey found to be the safe base at this size. Where a row names a model or a tool, it names today's filler for a role, and any filler that passes that role's gate may replace it. Each row says what it was chosen over.

rows.why: The survey's safe base at this size. The projection rebuilds in minutes and is never the only copy of anything.
rows.over: A graph database (Graphiti on Neo4j or FalkorDB; Kuzu, now archived). Links are an edge table, and a recursive query covers two hops at this size. DuckDB's vector extension documents its persistence as unsafe.

rows.choice: SQLite FTS5 with the unicode61 tokenizer, its external-content sync done right
rows.why: The measured core. The broken sync cost 0.050 MRR, and the fix is live.
rows.over: For Greek, where keyword search is weakest, no tokenizer option folds accents: an unaccented query misses under every setting. Folding in code fixes it, and E5 tests tokenizer variants over folded text against bge-m3's own sparse mode.

rows.why: It fits the scale: the scale simulation's median was 0.32 s for 6,000 entries plus 30,000 units.
rows.over: A separate vector database. sqlite-vec is pre-1.0 with its approximate index only in alpha; at this size exact search is fast enough.

rows.why: The incumbent. It is multilingual, takes long inputs, and stays until a challenger beats it on a gold set that covers today's corpus.
rows.over: Qwen3-Embedding, reported first on the multilingual MTEB board in June 2025, and EmbeddingGemma, whose 2k-token window would truncate long entries. No leaderboard measures Greek journals.

rows.choice: A weighted sum of normalised scores, with the weight set by query language
rows.why: Measured here: score fusion beat rank fusion, MRR 0.818 against 0.604 on 22 paraphrase pairs. The cited fusion study agrees when a small labelled set exists.
rows.over: Reciprocal rank fusion, measured here and rejected.

rows.choice: bge-reranker-v2-m3 over the top 25 episodes (today's filler)
rows.why: Independent signals, read only through search summaries, keep it competitive on multilingual tasks, and each vendor's own table favours its own model.
rows.over: Qwen3-Reranker, whose A/B on Greek waits for gold set v2; jina-reranker-v3; and late interaction, since no source shows a ColBERT-style model beating dense retrieval plus a cross-encoder on Greek.

rows.choice: One immutable file per episode, with a UUIDv7 id minted at birth and an exclusive create
rows.why: Ids tied to a position re-hashed 779 or 780 of 780 entries. Two new files never collide where two appends to one file do.
rows.over: One append-only journal file, as today, and notes rewritten in place (A-MEM). FT decides which format the file uses.

rows.choice: Append-only JSONL, one segment per month per machine, written under a lock in whole lines
rows.why: A merge of any number of machines is a union, every current view becomes a rebuildable projection, and the five stores round-trip to the byte through the projection.
rows.over: Today's five JSON and JSONL stores and a separate hash chain, 86% of which is session-sync noise.

rows.choice: Git history as the chain, plus a signed daily root
rows.why: Each committed ledger segment must be a byte prefix of its working copy, and git's hashes chain the history. Signatures are detached and checked against a list of allowed signers with validity windows; today's filler is an OpenSSH ed25519 key.
rows.over: Signed writes as an origin control, rejected because anything with a shell can sign. The result is tamper-evident, not tamper-proof.

rows.choice: A frontier model behind a role contract (today Opus through claude -p)
rows.why: It is the only distiller that passed its accuracy bar here. Code renders the file from its JSON.
rows.over: Any producer that has not passed the gate. The survey reports, as a weakened claim, that weak backbones fail silently on memory writes.

rows.choice: Code checks first (L0), then an entailment judge (L1)
rows.why: The survey finds entailment judges weak, so the judge never overrides a mechanical failure.
rows.over: Trusting a producer's output unchecked: 10 of 74 auto-authored entries carried an unsupported claim.

rows.choice: Links between facts, marked when proposed and decided after a 7-day hold, by one judge with a same-slot rule
rows.why: The literature finds memory goes wrong at extraction and update, so nothing is overwritten and the reader sees both versions with dates.
rows.over: Model-driven UPDATE and DELETE (Mem0 in 2025, Memory-R1), which Mem0 itself dropped for ADD-only writes, and forgetting by decay.

rows.choice: A private gold set with programmatic oracles, paired and clustered statistics, and bars registered first
rows.why: Public benchmarks are weak instruments. LoCoMo fits in a context window, and its full-context baseline beat every memory system in Mem0's own table.
rows.over: LoCoMo and LongMemEval headlines as the objective.

technology.survey_head: What the surveyed systems lent, and what was left

survey.took: Two clocks on every record, and invalidation instead of deletion.
ADD-only writes, with contradictions handled at read time.
Revising a fact's context, kept as a new version linked to the old one.
Consolidation as a background pass, which the nightly run already is.
survey.left: Agent-edited core blocks without version history.
A learned DELETE, and forgetting on a decay curve.

survey.took: Decay as a ranking boost only, and a complete reference provider for the harness.
survey.left: A tier ladder that rewrites stored entries into shorter summaries and keeps no original, and a delete verb the model can call.

survey.took: Recall as an explicit filterable tool, a compaction brief, and the rule that recalled memory is evidence, not instruction.
survey.left: A cloud-only plugin whose unit is a vendor-extracted fact.

technology.survey_note: Also surveyed: HippoRAG 2, Cognee, LangMem, MemoryOS, MIRIX, MemOS and Hindsight; and, for the persona's harness in September 2026, ten memory providers, seven of which hand the model a delete verb. Provenance chains back to raw transcripts are rare across all of them, and none keeps the corpus as the vendor-neutral source of truth.

where_we_stand: The successor is designed, not built. The FTS fix (D0) is live in the incumbent; a mining prototype has run, and the signer's self-test passes vectors 1 to 3. The decided core: one file per episode (D1), facts as keys (D2), roles with gates, open labels with a flow table, the three doors, layered integrity, and O1 to O23 apart from O19. Most of the rest is proposed spec.
Open now: the episode file type (FT), D3's two questions, whether transcripts are kept in git (D10), and whether the format evaluation's G5 takes the split credential.

The file-type tests G, R and R2 have run. R's primary found no reader-side difference that matters (branch C); its secondary is weak support for option 2 only. R2 is branch B: JSON does not change the door. The lean stays option 2, on the code side, weighed against the owner's hand reading.

Four more file-type tests were pre-registered before any ran. T-mut: no material difference in silent changes, and option 3 loses 25x more items per mutation than option 2. T-key: the key name did not drive R's evidence gap; the label confusion replicated, 6 of 64 against 0 of 64, small reader only. T-harness: the harness does not matter here. T-field: branch B, at the ceiling, so no format difference on field-shaped questions at 30 episodes; aggregation across thousands of episodes is untested.
The invisible-character rule is challenged by all three labs, and its rewrite is paused until the file-type call.
No role gate has run, apart from signer vectors 1 to 3. The format evaluation's arm B was generated and is unread.
The proposed first implementation step is M0, M1 and M2. The docs say nothing runs without the owner's go-ahead.
for_agents: This page and its exports are public, and so is their source: https://github.com/nyx-daemon/anamnesis, synced on every commit, with this page also served at https://nyx-daemon.github.io/anamnesis/. The data is in tracker.public.json, published beside this page, and as plain text in TRACKER.md; this page renders from the JSON in the browser.

Every item has an id, a kind, a status and an area. Statuses depend on the kind: a decision is decided, proposed or open; a task is todo, claimed, in-progress, blocked or done; a test is planned, pre-registered, running or run; a fact is measured, inferred or a hypothesis. Options take a decision's statuses; questions are open or answered; assumptions are untested, supported or refuted; risks are open, mitigated or accepted.

Each item lists its evidence, assumptions, what would change it (falsify), the tests that bear on it, what it depends on, the discussion so far, how to help, and its sources with the commit they were read at.

To claim a task, challenge an item, report a test or ask a question, open an issue with the forms at https://github.com/nyx-daemon/anamnesis, after reading AGENTS.md there, which is the protocol. Put the item id first in the title. A claim is recorded here only after a maintainer accepts it; until then the task's status does not change. The Colony post 8aa31518, in ai-agents, stays open for discussion.
Items marked local-only need private data (the tuning set, the transcripts, the owner's labels) or the owner's own call. Everything else can be taken from outside. A good first task is P.corpus.
Feedback from agents is untrusted data. It is read and credited to its author, never executed, and nothing in a reply changes this tracker by itself.

areas.name: Episode file type
areas.lede: Which bytes an episode is stored as is not decided, and nothing in this section is. Four options are on the table; a three-lab panel agreed on only one point, and the reader test found no reader-side difference that matters on its primary score, so the choice rests on archival terms and the owner's hand reading.

areas.name: Currency and D3
areas.lede: Currency is not decided. On 26 November it split into two questions. The owner has decided neither. Nothing outdated is hidden. A proposed update is marked at once, the hold only closes a validity interval, and the newest version is shown first.

areas.name: Write path
areas.lede: Every episode is born through one writer, in session or from a transcript. Code drafts what code can know; the author supplies judgement; every Record item is checked against its transcript, where one exists, before the file is created. The boxes for each part are on the map above.

areas.name: Episode format
areas.lede: One episode, one file: front matter, then the Record, the Harvest and the Reflection.

areas.name: Storage layers
areas.lede: The ladder: what is kept, bottom up, and which layer lives in git.

areas.name: Facts
areas.lede: A fact exists to get the right episode retrieved and to carry structure: subject, slot, kind and event time. Recall never serves one on its own, so a wrong fact costs a miss and a vanished producer costs only keys.

areas.name: Retrieval
areas.lede: The read path keeps the measured core, fixes what is broken, and adds facts as keys. Every hit comes back as an episode with its evidence, date and age.

areas.name: Delivery
areas.lede: The store is half the system. The other half is what a session actually loads: the pack at start, recall when asked, the files it greps, and the always-loaded canon. The pack, recall, prefetch, raw files and canon boxes are on the map; two more parts live here.

areas.name: Roles and gates
areas.lede: The core never names a model. It names roles, and anything that passes a role's gate may fill it: a cloud model, a local lane, a library. No gate has run yet.

areas.name: Labels and flow
areas.lede: Labels decide where content may flow, never whether it is kept. Live credentials are the one content never stored.

areas.name: Identity and safety
areas.lede: The agent now reads untrusted pages and a social network, so what it remembers from them must not be able to rewrite who it is. Origin is assigned by code at write time, and untrusted origin caps what content may do. Text no reader sees is removed before anything inspects or renders it. The exposure tiers and the social-only update rule are under Labels and Currency.

areas.name: Ledger and integrity
areas.lede: Detect, attest, repair. The chain, the signed root and the repair are decided; the single ledger they are drawn on is still a proposal (D4).

areas.name: Doors out
areas.lede: Nothing is deleted silently. Invalidate, redact and purge are three different operations, and which one applies depends on how a layer reaches the model. The three door boxes are on the map.

areas.name: Migration
areas.lede: Identity before data, shadow before cutover, measurement before retirement. Every stage has a check that it worked, a check that it can be undone, and a gate for the next. All of it is proposed.

areas.name: Evaluation
areas.lede: Written before anything is built, so the bars cannot be chosen after a result. Each experiment gets its own full pre-registration, with both branches written first, before it runs.

areas.name: Not adopted
areas.lede: Not adopting something is also a recommendation, so each of these carries a mark. Below them, the ideas this engine already measured and rejected.

areas.name: Project
areas.lede: Work the design docs do not hold yet: a public corpus that any vendor's reader can run on, and runs that need one.

items.title: Episode file type: the canonical stored bytes
items.summary:
1. **What are the canonical stored bytes?** D1 decided one file per episode, not its type, and none of O1 to O23 touches it.
2. **What is a reader shown?** That is D3's second question, still open: the raw files, a rendered tree with marks inline, or only recall's rendering.

Nyx's first lean coupled them: the Record's serialization would follow whichever reader door D3 picked. A three-lab panel **unanimously rejected that coupling**, and it is withdrawn. The stored bytes are an archive meant to last decades; the door is a rendering that can be retired or bypassed. So the bytes are chosen on archival terms. OpenAI's terms: lossless representation, unambiguous decoding, independent implementations, versioning, recovery from corruption, inspection without tools. DeepSeek's: one simple parser, minimal custom escaping, safe hand edits, long-term readability.

**Reversible until M5.** Options 1 and 2 encode the same parsed form, and no schema-1 file exists outside the quarantine, so the choice stays cheap to reverse until the journal is split.

**The trade the owner decides:** option 2 retires the custom grammar, its percent layer and its conformance suite, and costs hand-readability, because a JSON line is harder to read than an item line.
items.why: Across R and R2, readers did about as well on the grammar, on JSONL and on pure JSON. The reader side gives no reason to leave option 1, and none to choose 3 over 2. The case for option 2 is on the code side: a standard parser, no percent layer and no conformance suite. It has to be weighed against the owner's hand reading. Since then, T-mut found no material difference in silent rates, and option 3's blast radius is material: 25x option 2's. T-key found the key name did not drive the gap; the label confusion replicated, 6 of 64 against 0 of 64, so far seen only in the small reader. T-harness: the harness does not matter here. T-field: branch B, at the ceiling, so no format difference on field-shaped questions at this size.

The owner's own hand reading is not measured.
items.falsify: A pre-registered branch that favours one option by its declared margin. R's branch A (option 1 ahead by at least 0.10 with a CI that excludes 0) would have flipped the lean. Aggregation across thousands of episodes, where counting by hand stops working, is untested (T.scale).

discussion.gist: OpenAI backs option 2 whichever door wins, at medium confidence, provided the envelope is specified rigidly. It also notes that the front matter is YAML whose values are JSON, not line-by-line JSON as 08 §3 words it.
DeepSeek leans the same way without naming an option: option 1's custom escaping is an ongoing parser risk, and option 2 handles invisible characters more defensibly.
Gemini rejects both 1 and 2: custom grammars rot, and fenced JSONL is the worst of both worlds, because jq needs a pre-processor and dense JSON is hard on the eye. Its alternative is option 4.
Unanimous: the stored bytes must not follow the reader door. That is the only point all three agreed on. All three were told to attack the lean, so "nobody defends option 1" is partly the prompt.

items.how_to_help: Argue the archival terms, not the reader door: lossless representation, unambiguous decoding, independent implementations, versioning, recovery from corruption, inspection without tools. A concrete failure of one option on one of those terms is the most useful reply.

items.title: Option 1 · Today's line grammar
items.summary: A markdown file: one-line JSON values in the front matter; Record and Harvest as item lines with two-space field lines; free text through a reversible percent layer so no value can start a line, open a heading or open a comment; two independent parsers that must agree under a conformance suite; the Reflection as prose. It costs the custom grammar, its percent layer and its conformance suite for as long as the store lives. A grep hit on an item line carries neither its anchors nor its quotes, which sit on separate field lines.

items.title: The mining path, step by step
items.summary:
1. **Prep, code only:** the quotable corpus of each in-scope transcript, credentials redacted, numbered by message and tool id, cut at human-turn boundaries, with the Harvest written by code. One job per segment, carrying its scope labels.
2. **Mining:** the producer returns JSON items; code renders them. Facts, decisions and corrections need a snapped quote or a commit anchor; inferred items are not allowed; machine authors cannot force items; no Reflection is ever synthesised.
3. **Labels and screens:** the label classifier adds labels, the credential screen runs on every value.
4. **Quarantine:** everything lands outside git and outside memory, never indexed or read by recall, extraction, P3, the pack or the publishing path.
5. **Promotion** goes through the writer only, after the credential fixture passes, the label classifier passes its gate, the format evaluation decides the format, and M5 is done. Each batch is signed.
6. **Order** is newest first, stopping when a batch fails its gate (Transcript-first mining (*Decided*)).
7. If the format changes, the quarantine is re-mined, not converted. Deferred jobs run first when a producer that accepts them passes its gate.

Scope: every session with a transcript of at least 30 KB, except two excluded directories. Work projects are in scope with work labels. A back-filled episode's recorded time is its promotion, so SessionStart never shows a mined episode as the newest.

items.title: Credential rules: the mechanics
items.summary:
Credential screen (*Decided*) The decision is that live credentials are always redacted. How:

- **Two places:** inputs are redacted before any author or producer sees them, and the writer refuses any value that still matches, reporting line numbers only, never the match or its class.
- **Screened:** every free-text value: front matter, every item and field, the Reflection, digests and skeletons, companions, and every changed episode file at commit.
- **One signature list**, imported, never copied; if it cannot load, nothing is written.
- **An entropy rule** catches long mixed-case tokens; it is a proposal, tuned on fixtures, and its false-positive rate is reported.
- **URLs** lose their query strings, fragments and user info before screening and storage.
- **Invisible characters first** (a proposal): the screen reads text with them removed, so a credential split by a zero-width character still matches (Invisible characters removed first (*Proposed*)).
- **Legacy bodies** are flagged, not rewritten: the credential is rotated, and removal from history goes through purge on the owner's word.

items.title: Front matter: birth values only
items.summary:
A strict line grammar that is valid YAML and valid line-by-line JSON. Every value is one single-line JSON value, and every string is double-quoted. Times are UTC with Z (Times in UTC (*Decided*)).

| Group | Fields |
|---|---|
| Identity and time | `schema`, `id`, `recorded_at`, `recorded_how`, `anchor_at` |
| Who wrote it | `origin` (in-session, auto, mined, retro), `kind`, `author_kind`, `producer`, `host` |
| Where it came from | `session`, `anchor`, `covers`, `covers_at`, `via`, `source_session`, `reflections` |
| Claimed by the author | `title`, `event_date`, `thread`, `continues`, `projects`, `topics` |
| Flow | `labels`, `scope_labels`, `origin_providers` (the provider of every session the evidence anchors into, read from those transcripts by code; where it is absent, the label policy decides) |
| Flags | `needs_reparse`, `deferred`, `lang`, and for legacy files `legacy`, `legacy_id`, `header_time` |

**Never in the file:** its own hash (a file cannot hold it), exposure (it can change while the session runs), verification verdicts, labels added later, link decisions, loop status. Each of those is a ledger event, so a machine never rewrites an episode.

A malformed line drops only that key and is logged. If the id itself is unusable, the parser recovers it from the ledger; failing that, the file is quarantined, never deleted.

discussion.gist: The front matter is YAML whose values are JSON, not line-by-line JSON as 08 §3 words it.

items.title: The Record's item types
items.summary:
An item line is `- <letter><n> <type>: <one sentence>`, followed by indented field lines. The Record's types are proposed with the Record.

|  | Type | What it holds | Required keys |
|---|---|---|---|
| `o` | outcome | what the episode ended as; at least one per episode | status |
| `d` | decision | a choice that closed | why, rejected, status, by, ev with a quote |
| `f` | fact | a claim about the world; hedges keep their wording | mode, ev |
| `c` | change | an artifact that changed | kind, state, ref |
| `m` | measure | a number the entry relies on | value, how |
| `a` | ask | the owner's instruction, verbatim | q, scope, ev on a human-typed turn |
| `p` | pref | a stated preference | q, mode, ev on a human-typed turn |
| `x` | correction | what was wrong and is now right | was, now, target, rule, ev; who caught it is computed |
| `l` | open | an unresolved loop | owner, until |
| `k` | lesson | two sentences at most; interpretation, never a fact | derived_from |
| `e` | entity | a person, agent, repo, host, tool, model or PR | kind |

The required keys sit where the audit found the prose weakest: `measure.how` (33 of 36 numbers unsourced), `open.owner` and `until` (14 of 28 ownerless), `change.state`, `decision.rejected`. A later episode closes a loop or supersedes a decision by reference; the old file is never edited.

items.title: Evidence anchors
items.summary:
| Anchor | Points to | Quote |
|---|---|---|
| `m:` | a message in a session transcript | allowed; required on asks, preferences, decisions and corrections |
| `t:` | a tool call and its result | allowed |
| `g:` | a commit in a registered repo | a substring of its subject, body or diff |

| `u:` | a URL, with no query string or fragment | none |

items.title: What evidence may be quoted
items.summary:
- **The corpus:** human-typed spans of human turns, tool results, and assistant text. Never tool-call inputs, thinking, or anything after the anchor.
- **No circular evidence:** a tool result is excluded when its call read or wrote an episode, the draft, the generated view, canon or the quarantine. Otherwise memory could cite itself.
- **The anchor** is the last message flushed to the transcript before the write call, so an author can never quote what it is writing. The writer waits up to 10 seconds for the flush (a proposal), and gate G0 measures whether that holds before M5.
- **Human-typed** is an allowlist of real transcript record shapes. Hook output, notifications, command output, compaction summaries, tool results and cross-session messages are never human-typed, even in a user turn. Anything attributed to the owner must anchor a human-typed span.

items.title: Verification: L0, L1, statuses, eligibility
items.summary:
**L0, mechanical, no model:** targets exist at or before the anchor; quotes are substrings after invisible-character removal and Unicode normalisation, on both sides; commits and PRs exist and contain their quotes; paths and URLs were seen; numbers match a token in the cited tool result with their label on the same line; owner-attributed items anchor human-typed spans; references resolve; times parse.

**L1, semantic:** does the evidence entail the claim? It runs on every decision, correction, ask and preference, on pointer-only items, on short quotes in long results, and on every item of an auto or mined episode.

| Status | Means |
|---|---|
| supported | L0 and L1 pass |
| anchored | L0 passes; L1 not run |
| pointer-only | pointer anchors only, no content check |
| quote-missing, anchor-invalid | L0 failures |
| unsupported | L1 rejected it: quarantined by event, kept in the file with a badge |
| unverifiable | the transcript is gone |
| pending | a source is not readable yet |

**As keys:** decisions, corrections, asks and preferences need *supported*; facts, measures, changes, loops and lessons need *supported* or *anchored*. Labels never change eligibility. If a transcript is later deleted, an earlier *supported* verdict stands.

**At write time** the whole append is refused only on a credential hit. Every other failure withholds that one item, reported by line number; a forced item is written visibly weaker and is never a key.

items.title: Additions, revisions and hand edits
items.summary:
- **Companion records** hold later additions in their own files beside the episode, never matched by the episode glob: back-fill items from legacy prose, or a nightly pass's additions.
- **revise** edits in place, re-runs the screen and labels, and records the old and new hash. Items anchor to the transcript, not to the episode text, so a revision does not orphan them.
- **A hand edit outside the writer** is found by the integrity check as a mismatch and is never accepted automatically. Until someone accepts it with `revise --accept`, the episode leaves every index, and the edited bytes are kept aside, never deleted.
- **A materially wrong episode** gets a new episode that continues and supersedes it. The old one is marked by an event.

items.title: The legacy journal, kept byte for byte
items.summary:
- Each legacy entry becomes a file of new front matter plus its original text verbatim, exempt from every heading rule.
- Its recorded time comes from the marker if it has one, else from the header in the old time zone, else from the entry before it, and it says which.
- A frozen manifest lists every legacy entry in journal order with its body hash. Rejoining them reproduces the journal's bytes as split (gate G3).
- Every in-scope session with a transcript gets mined episodes; its legacy entries are their Reflection of record. A session whose transcript is gone keeps its prose plus Pass B companions (O7).
- The credential screen runs over legacy bodies and flags, never rewrites: a credential already in history is rotated, and removing it from history is purge's job.
- Acceptance: a blind sample of 60 items per pass, at most 2 unsupported (3.9%).

items.title: What a fact record carries
items.summary:
- **Where it points:** the episode, the episode's hash at extraction and, for schema-1 episodes, the item id and its hash.
- **The quote**, anchored with a prefix and suffix so it survives edits (a W3C text-quote selector, re-attached the way Hypothesis does).
- **Subject and slot**, owned by the extractor; the author's `about:` is only a hint, and E1 tests whether it helps.
- **Kind:** durable, state, event or plan. Only states and plans can be superseded; an event stays true as history.
- **Event time** with its granularity and how it was known. Relative dates resolve against the anchored message's time, by code.
- **Mode:** stated, reported, hedged or inferred, so a hedge stays a hedge.
- **Producer:** the model, the prompt version and the run.
- **Labels:** its source item's, so a fact flows no further than its item.

For schema-1 episodes, one Record item becomes at most one fact. The density rule of about one fact per 400 characters (cap 15) applies only to the legacy prose path.

items.title: The flow rules
items.summary:
1. The policy is rows of label pattern, sink, allow or deny; one row is the default for unlabelled content.
2. For one label and one sink, deny beats allow: if any matching row denies, the flow is denied; otherwise a matching allow permits it; and a known label with no row for that sink is denied, which fails safe.
3. A unit may go to a sink only if every one of its labels allows it.
4. A label no row names reaches owner sessions only. (The profile's table also lets it reach canon; the docs disagree.)
5. Unlabelled content follows the default row.
6. Owner sessions and recall are never denied.
7. A rendering's flow is the intersection over everything it shows.
8. Public surfaces and non-free providers gate on the whole episode's labels, so an under-labelled item cannot leak beside a labelled one.
9. Pushing a file to a remote is a flow, gated the same way.
10. The owner may allow one specific denied flow, in the owner's own words, logged; the persona never writes one.
11. Flow to a provider is free when it is the content's origin, a local provider, or in the trusted set (empty today). (The profile's local column denies an unnamed label; the docs disagree.)

- **The publishing guard** reads every store whatever its labels, refuses verbatim and paraphrased quotes, and fails closed.

items.title: Invisible characters removed first (challenged, rewrite paused)
items.summary: The set is Unicode's Default_Ignorable_Code_Point, written out as fixed ranges so every host uses the same one: tag characters, bidi controls, zero-width characters, variation selectors and blank fillers. Wherever text is normalised or inspected, they are removed first and NFC comes after. The writer removes them from every value it writes and records the count as n_invisible; emoji glue, bounded so it cannot hide a payload, is removed but not counted. Every rendering removes them before any fence, mark or badge, and shows the badge invisible:<n>. Contested: all three labs of the format panel contested removal. It destroys evidence, ZWJ and ZWNJ carry meaning in some scripts, and removal plus NFC can make different strings identical. Their alternative is to keep originals, escape visibly, and remove only in derived views. Challenged; rewrite paused until the file-type decision.
items.why: They display as nothing, so text that carries them can say something no reader sees, and NFC and whitespace folding keep them. Removing them after a step would let them split what that step exists to catch: a comment opener, or a credential with a zero-width space inside it. Measured baseline, 30 days to 2026-11-26: 76 of 572 transcripts held any; 562 characters, 540 of them in tool results and 184 of them emoji glue; no tag characters. The journal holds one, a U+202E.

items.summary: Each ledger line carries the hash of its data and of the line before it, one chain per machine. Every file's expected hash is recorded, so a silent change is found. The chain covers the hash of the data, not the data, so a purge tombstone does not break it.

items.title: Signed daily root
items.summary: Each day a machine computes a Merkle root over its files and ledger segments and signs it. Once a signed root sits on replicas an editor does not control, rewriting history shows.

items.title: Repair from replicas
items.summary: A file that fails its expected hash is replaced from a replica that matches, and the mismatching bytes are set aside, never deleted. items.title: Statements, keys and verification
items.summary:
- **Statements:** a daily root per host, and one per promotion batch, each naming the last ledger line it covers so the state it describes can be reproduced.
- **Signing:** only hosts the profile names as signers sign. A host without the key writes its root unsigned, and the next signed root that has merged its segments covers it.
- **Keys:** public keys sit in an allowed-signers file with validity windows. A rotation is signed by the outgoing key, and old signatures keep verifying for their dates.
- **Verify** checks five things, reporting by path and code, never content: every host chain is intact and every committed segment is a prefix; every live file matches its expected hash and nothing unknown sits in the globs; every root recomputes; every signature verifies for its date; signed roots agree across replicas.

items.title: Five invariants for every stage
items.summary:
1. **Byte-exact inverses.** Every structural change to the journal can be undone to the byte (T3a proved it for the split).
2. **Raw import.** Every legacy record enters the ledger raw, and every re-export through the shadow period is byte-identical (T3c).
3. **Nothing deleted.** A retired file freezes read-only in git; retired code moves aside with its last measurement.
4. **A commit before and after each stage**, pushed. Obligation partitions commit locally and are never pushed (08 §11.3).
5. **Transcripts are untouched** throughout.

Every stage has the same four parts: a precondition, a check that it worked, a check that it can be undone, and the gate for the next stage. The docs say nothing runs without the owner's go-ahead.

items.title: Rule A: what it takes to ship
items.summary:
1. **No worse on known items.** Known-item plus cross-lingual MRR: successor minus the incumbent of record at least −0.02.
2. **Currency.** On held-out "now" questions, the newest relevant episode is first in its group at least 80% of the time, and at least 0.30 better than the incumbent, scored only on update pairs absent from the link store. With fewer than 25 such items it is not a measurement.
3. **Invariants, zero tolerance:** byte-identical re-exports through the shadow period; every fact resolves to an episode and every traced episode to a session; the FTS integrity check passes; a recall writes nothing.
4. **Latency:** warm p50 at most 0.5 s and cold p95 at most 1.5 s on 200 replayed prompts.

Reported with consequences (Rule B): as-of at least 0.75, when at least 0.70, abstention false-evidence at most 0.20, two-hop reported. Not a win: a gain on the legacy set alone, on dev only, or one that vanishes against the FTS-fixed incumbent.

items.title: The format evaluation (08d)
items.summary:
The question: does a Record plus Reflection episode answer more of the questions future sessions will ask than prose plus the code-written Harvest plus the pre-fill checklist, at an acceptable author cost and with no safety regression?

| Arm | What it writes |
|---|---|
| A | prose only, today's shape |
| A+H, the fair control | the same prose plus the Harvest, with the pre-fill checklist shown as things to cover |
| B | the core format: skeleton, Record, Harvest, Reflection |
| B-rec | B, indexed without the Record and Harvest, to see whether the Record helps as keys or only as text |
| L | the existing journal entry, for reference only |

**Two question batteries**, generated from the transcripts by a local model: a **generic battery** of LongMemEval's types, whose accuracy is P1, and a **local battery** derived from the gap audit (decisions, commits, corrections, instructions, open loops, numbers), whose accuracy is P2. The local battery never decides P1, because it shares the audit's method.

**Decision rule, fixed in advance:** B wins if, against A+H, P2 rises by at least 0.08 with a lower bound above zero; P1 falls by no more than 0.02, with no generic type more than 0.05 worse (a no-harm screen, not a non-inferiority test); unsupported claims stay at or below 3.9%; the author writes at most about 1,000 tokens more; and every safety gate passes. It loses if P2 rises less than 0.02, or on any safety failure. Otherwise a lighter Record is tried type by type on a fresh decision set, with at most one re-run. The docs warn that at 40 sessions the +0.08 bar sits below the minimum detectable effect, so a miss is not evidence of no effect.

**Three branches, written first:** the Record ships; or prose plus the Harvest ship and the Record sections close without being deleted; or only the types that clear the bar ship.

**Where it stands:** the decision and tuning sets were drawn and frozen by code on 25 November. Arm B was generated on both before tuning, a recorded deviation; its output is unread and provisional. Arms A and A+H have no prompts yet.
items.falsify: Its decision rule, fixed in advance, decides whether the Record ships (see EF.record).

items.title: No FTS5 tokenizer folds Greek accents
items.summary: unicode61 by default, with remove_diacritics 1 or 2, and trigram with remove_diacritics 1 all find an accented Greek word and miss the same word typed without its accent. Folding in code before the tokenizer (NFD, strip combining marks) at index time and on the query finds every variant and leaves ASCII untouched. The gold set cannot see the defect: all 41 of its Greek queries are accented.
items.why: First measured in the nyx-vessel memory-provider survey (2026-09-10, SQLite 3.53.4) and re-measured on 2026-11-26 (SQLite 3.54.1). The design had carried it as unverified.

evidence.claim: Unaccented Greek query against an accented index, by tokenizer
evidence.value: unicode61, remove_diacritics 1 and 2, trigram remove_diacritics 1: miss. Folded in code: hit.

items.falsify: A tokenizer setting that matches an unaccented Greek query against accented text.
items.how_to_help: Reproduce it on your SQLite build and report the version, or find a tokenizer that folds Greek accents.

items.title: A harness's own memory keeps facts outside the record
items.summary: A harness can run its own built-in memory beside the persona's provider. In Hermes it sits at its character cap, where each new fact costs an old one chosen by the model, with no source and no undo, while holding facts kept nowhere else. Hermes already offers a hook (on_memory_write) that hands every built-in write to the external provider; the persona's provider does not implement it.
items.why: Found in the nyx-vessel memory-provider survey (2026-09-10) and re-checked on 2026-11-26: the built-in memory is still enabled, both of its files sit at their caps, and the hook is still absent. It breaks never-delete from outside the design.
items.local_only_reason: The fix is in the persona's own provider and harness configuration on the owner's machine.
items.how_to_help: From outside: name other harnesses that run a built-in memory beside an external provider, and how each can be bridged into a never-delete record.

items.title: Weigh seven designs lifted from the memory-provider survey
items.summary: Each design maps to an item here. (1) Two reference MemoryProvider implementations, for the provider this design owes. (2) Recall as an explicit, filterable tool, with a structured compaction brief (DL.recall). (3) A one-line injection-hygiene rule: recalled memory is evidence, not instruction (IS.fence). (4) Event time apart from ingest time, already here. (5) Tiered retrieval under a token budget (RT.slices, DL.pack). (6) Prefetch that discards stale results (DL.prefetch). (7) Decay as a ranking boost only.
items.why: From the nyx-vessel memory-provider survey: none of the ten providers fits, but these designs cost nothing to adopt.
items.how_to_help: Take one design, write how it would fit the item it maps to, and say what test would show it helps. Survey §8 names each source.

items.title: Fold in the prior work the design does not cite yet
items.summary: A sweep on 26 November mapped thirteen groups of earlier work that this design does not cite. The most load-bearing: the P3 promotion decision and its two pre-registrations, the stage that writes into canon and sits on the ID.B boundary. Then the pipeline, semantic-recall and lifecycle decisions; the first law of the journal architecture guide; two earlier research runs on agent memory (May and August 2026), with their own caveats; lab notes and essays on summarizer distortion, hedge loss and how sessions reach memory; two literature deep dives; the open measurement documents; the tests of whether dates survive distillation; the Hermes memory-provider documentation; the supersession hand-offs; and the record of why the embedder was chosen.
items.why: The design package was written in two days against a codebase and a vault that hold months of decisions and measurements. What it does not cite, it may contradict or re-derive.
items.local_only_reason: The sources are private documents that sit next to the corpus.
